...since the discoveries and conclusions of human reason—even those that are now common and well-known—were new and unusual at that time, everything was full of all kinds of fables, enigmas, parables, and comparisons. Through these, a method of teaching was sought, rather than a trick of concealment; this was for the unrefined human minds of that time, which were impatient with, and almost incapable of, any subtlety unless it could be perceived by the senses. For just as *hieroglyphs* <note>original: *Hieroglyphica*</note> are older than letters, so *parables* <note>original: *parabolae*</note> are older than logical arguments. And even now, if anyone wishes to shed new light on any subject into human minds, and to do so smoothly and without harshness, they must follow exactly the same path and seek help from comparisons. Therefore, the *Wisdom of the Ancient Age* <note>original: *Sapientia prisci seculi*</note> was either great or fortunate: great, if the figure or trope was intentionally devised; fortunate, if men, while doing something else, provided the material and occasion for such noble contemplations. — Nor can I be unaware that this matter has been attempted by others; but yet, to speak my mind freely and without disdain, the beauty and power of the subject has almost perished from such labors, however great and painstaking they were. But because the discourse is of Nature and the Vessel at once, I and all philosophers follow the advice given to us by the son of Sendivogius <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636) was a famous Polish alchemist; "the son" likely refers to a follower or a pseudonymous work attributed to his lineage.</note> *t)*: “Look,” (he says) “how the mother protects and encloses her fruit, the child, and nourishes and maintains it between the **waters of the amnion and chorion** <note>original Latin: *Amnii und chorii*. The Seal <note>original Latin: *Sigillum*. This refers to the "Seal of Hermes," the airtight closing of the alchemical glass.</note>.)

> ...conflict, until finally one part receives help and succor from its external element, whereupon the **opposing part** <note>original Latin: *pars opposita*</note> must yield and leave the victory to the stronger. Following this is the destruction or separation of the entire substance, such that a new form lies before one’s eyes, which has been generated **through corruption** <note>original Latin: *per corruptionem*. To indicate its heavenly origin, it is designated with a circle and a perpendicular line 🜔 <note>An alchemical symbol resembling the globus cruciger, often associated with Antimony or the Earth</note>, though it also simultaneously has a diametrical line 🜕 <note>The symbol for Salt</note>, in such a way that these two lines, when connected together, represent the figure of the **Verdigris of the Wise** ⊕ <note>A circle containing a cross; in alchemy, this symbol often represents the Earth or the purified mineral Verdigris</note>, which displays the beginning and the completion of all secrets in nature; for the cross within the circle contains within itself the four elements. — This figure was crowned with a cross, where the round circle represents the **Vitriol** <term>vitriol</term> <note>A category of sulfate minerals, highly valued in alchemy for their acidic properties and seen as a key to the philosopher's stone</note>, and the cross—as **Basilius Valentinus** <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, supposedly a Benedictine monk, though his writings likely date to the 16th century</note> says—represents the chariot of the goddess **Fortuna**, upon which she carries the salvation of wisdom to the men of God. Now, whoever knows and understands how to use our vitriol, our **niter** <term>niter</term> <note>Saltpeter, often associated with the "universal spirit" in alchemy</note>, our **electrum** <note>An alloy of gold and silver, or a symbolic "philosophical" metal</note>, and our **double Saturn** <term>double Saturn</term> <note>In alchemy, "Saturn" is the name for Lead; "double Saturn" often refers to a purified or dual nature of the metal or its association with the planet Saturn</note>—which at their innermost core are all nothing but salt—will learn to see what a magnificent thing salt is. ### Second Part. Third Section.

Basilius Valentinus <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist, though many works under this name were likely written later by publishers like Johann Thölde.</note> says: “Two stars are given to man, which are meant to lead him. ...matter upon which Nature has demonstrated her highest art.” Magister Erbinäus von Brandau. (*) (Regarding the judgment of this, see Fictuld’s *Testing Stone* <note>Original: *Probierstein*, a famous 18th-century alchemical bibliography by Hermann Fictuld.</note>, Part 2). Therefore, the philosophers describe their Stone as a gold that has been ripened to the highest degree of perfection; for gold is similar to a plant, which does not produce its seed until it has reached full maturity; thus, gold also produces its seed or the <term>tincture</term> <note>In alchemy, a tincture is a concentrated essence capable of transmuting metals or healing the body.</note> once it has attained its perfect ripening. Michael Sendivogius <note>A famous Polish alchemist and physician (1566–1636).</note> in <term>The New Chemical Light</term> <note>Original Latin: *Novum Lumen Chymicum*.</note>, Treatise X, page 429 and following. Also in the <term>Chemical Theater</term> <note>Original Latin: *Theatrum Chemicum*, a massive compendium of alchemical writings.</note>, Volume IV, page 492. One must only take the old <term>Hermetic axiom</term> <note>A fundamental principle of the Hermetic tradition, which seeks to understand the secrets of nature and spirit.</note> into careful consideration:

> We have no other gold than common gold, but it is not called ours until it has been vivified by our living water. <note>Original Latin: “Non habemus aliud aurum, quam aurum vulgi, sed id non prius dicitur, nostrum, quam sit viuificatum, per aquam nostram viuam.”</note>

that is:

> “We have no other gold than the gold of the common man, but this is not called ours until it has been made alive with our living water.”

The expression <term>living water</term> <note>Often referring to the "Philosophical Mercury," a solvent believed to dissolve gold and release its inner spirit.</note> is of great importance, and it is the very high secret of whose excellence even the beginning younger brothers in our assemblies are informed long before they reach the level where this hidden truth is fully revealed to them.

### §. 5.

Now we wish, for the sake of completeness, to hear how the aforementioned [principle], so highly praised by **Pontanus**, <note>Johann Pontanus, a famous and somewhat mysterious alchemical author often cited in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note> [manifests]
> "...in their qualities and in regard to the degrees of perfection which give existence to the forms." <note>This fragment completes the sentence from the previous page: "it is nonetheless different in qualities..."</note>

Through these beautiful words, a truth is simultaneously elucidated that might be better addressed further below. It is nothing less than incomprehensible how a **fixed body**, having first been made volatile through the proper addition of related **volatile spirits**, can nevertheless bind these same spirits once more, making them fixed and resistant to fire. Indeed, even a naturally volatile body has the power to bind another body that is also volatile. 

The first case is more easily understood, since every fixed body preserves the seed and the grain of its fire-resistance <term>fixity</term> <note>The quality of a substance that allows it to withstand intense heat without evaporating or changing.</note> indestructibly within the very center of its structure. But that the latter can achieve this same effect occurs through the **attractive power** hidden within them. This is what is termed a "consubstantial" <note>Sharing the same fundamental essence or substance.</note>, inseparable union. See **S. Jugel's** <note>Johann Gottfried Jugel (1707–1786), a German mining official and alchemical writer known for his practical approach to "experimental chemistry."</note> *Experimental Chemistry*, Part 1, Class III, Note 1, § 85. He proves this in the same work, Theorem 2, Explanation 4, § 8 and following, using the example of **spirit of wine** <note>High-proof alcohol (ethanol).</note> and the **spirit of sal ammoniac** <note>A solution of ammonia. When the "spirits" (vapors) of alcohol and ammonia interact with certain acids or salts, they can form solid precipitates, illustrating how two "volatile" things become "fixed."</note>. 

**N.B.** <note>abbreviation for the Latin *nota bene*, meaning "note well."</note> It would be desirable if the gentlemen physicians would earnestly apply themselves to these two spirits

### §. 5.

Now nothing remains for me but to speak of the **abbreviation of the Great Work** <term>Great Work: the "Magnum Opus," or the full process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term>; to which end I call upon the great Raymond Lull a) <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan polymath and philosopher to whom many alchemical treatises were later attributed</note> once more for assistance, who speaks thus of it:

i) P. 63.

a) In the *Accurate Letter* in Manget <note>Jean-Jacques Manget (1652–1742), editor of the *Bibliotheca Chemica Curiosa*, a famous collection of alchemical texts</note>, cited place, p. 866. a.
<note>original Latin: "Ex plumbo philosophorum extrahitur quoddam oleum aurei coloris vel quasi..."</note>
From the **lead of the philosophers** <term>lead of the philosophers: a symbolic starting material, often associated with antimony or the raw, "chaotic" state of matter</term> is extracted a certain oil of golden color, or nearly so: With which, if you sublimate the mineral, vegetable, animal, or mixed stone, after the first **fixation** <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat</term>, three or four times, it will relieve you of all the labor of **solutions** and **coagulations** <note>The repetitive cycles of dissolving and solidifying that usually take months or years</note>. ->§. 6.<-

### Closing Speech.

Now come, you dear friends, venerable fathers! You artists, of whom God says through the prophet \*) that he created you to blow upon the coal fire, so that you may bring forth your material for the <term>Work</term> <note>the *Magnum Opus* or Great Work of alchemy</note>. Now come with me to the inward-vaulted temple consecrated to Divine Wisdom. Ask and knock; God will hear you, and command Nature, who is its true gatekeeper, to allow you to open the temple’s hidden trapdoors: To give you her twofold key. But walk cautiously, so that you do not defile this consecrated ground, and bow down in all humility, so that you do not stain your silver-gray hair with the royal purple <note>A reference to the *rubedo* or "reddening" stage, the final and highest phase of the alchemical process, often associated with royalty and perfection</note> hanging around above; you will regret it. Carry with deliberation your twofold sacrifice, one after the other, onto the altar artistically raised in the center: Take, like Prometheus \*\*), the tinder, and burn cautiously,

<meta>This page transitions from the liturgical repetitions and scriptural praises found on the previous page to a formal "Errata" list. ## Errata.

Page 69, note i) instead of "lobyaigyptioi" <note>original Greek: λοβυαιγύπτιοι</note> read: "libyaigyptioi" <note>original Greek: λιβυαιγύπτιοι, a term referring to the Liby-Egyptians</note>.
Page 97, note q) instead of "deinyon" <note>original Greek: δεινύων</note> read: "deiknyon" <note>original Greek: δεικνύων, meaning "pointing out" or "showing"</note>.
Page 114, line 12: instead of "infallible's" read: infallible.
Page 213, line 14: instead of "allmeine" read: "allgemeine" <note>the German word for "general" or "universal"</note>.
Pages 340, 346, and 347: instead of "measurement" <note>original German: Messung</note> one should always read: "wafting" <note>original German: Wehung. In mystical or alchemical contexts, this refers to a divine breath, a spiritual breeze, or the movement of the Spirit, which the author prefers here over the more clinical "measurement."</note>.

The kind reader will please excuse that the newly added notes were not initially distinguished by an asterisk (*). However, those who compare this improved edition with the first will easily notice the improvements.

It concludes with a note to the reader explaining that new additions to this revised version were not explicitly marked but should be self-evident upon comparison.</summary>
